item.title: Large Models and Agent Applications
item.description:
Focusing on large language models and agents, this direction centers on building decision-making capabilities within the closed loop of “perception — planning — execution”: enabling models to understand task goals, invoke external tools and knowledge, and deliver measurable, deployable intelligent applications in vertical scenarios.

Direction Overview

The lab treats large models as composable cognitive and decision-making components, conducting research on single-agent capability enhancement, multi-agent collaboration, and domain knowledge injection, with systematic validation in scenarios such as culture and tourism and education. Related practice includes application explorations such as the university culture-and-tourism large model “Yijian Boguan: Zhihui Wanxiang” (a large model for culture and tourism).

Research Topics

  • Model vertical applications: application modeling, prompt engineering, and effectiveness evaluation of large models
  • Enhance single agents: task planning, tool use, and external knowledge retrieval augmentation
  • Organize multi-agent collaboration: role division, task allocation, and negotiation mechanisms
  • Control reasoning processes: multi-step reasoning, decision trajectories, and controllable generation for complex tasks
  • Integrate deployable systems: interface specifications, safety boundaries, and human-agent collaboration workflows

Key Challenges

  • Planning failures: ambiguous task goals and heterogeneous tool interfaces in open environments
  • Collaboration consistency: conflict resolution and cost control across multi-agent systems
  • Knowledge fusion: integrating domain knowledge with general capabilities and suppressing hallucinations
  • Missing evaluation: lack of unified, reproducible protocols for application effectiveness

Technical Approach

  • Characterize task graphs: express planning with task graphs / workflows, reduce hallucinations via retrieval and tool use
  • Build evaluation loops: design observable execution logs and evaluation metrics to support iterative optimization
  • Construct demonstration systems: connect data, models, and user interfaces in vertical scenarios

item.title: Low-Light Vision Enhancement
item.description:
Targeting degraded scenarios such as low illumination, high noise, and complex lighting, this direction studies the restoration, enhancement, and robust feature representation of visual information, so that enhanced results are not only “better looking” but also serve downstream tasks such as focusing, matching, optical flow, and reconstruction.

Direction Overview

Low-light imaging commonly suffers from low signal-to-noise ratio, drowned-out details, and color distortion. The lab advances along two lines: enhancement-reconstruction and task-driven research. One line improves the visual quality of images/videos; the other learns feature representations that are more friendly to downstream geometric and motion estimation. Related work covers low-light optical flow (e.g., CEDFlow, latent-feature-supervised siamese networks) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) General Program project “Research on Light Field Feature Computation Enhancement Theory and Methods for Low-Light Autofocusing”.

Research Topics

  • Restore image quality: low-light image / video enhancement, denoising, and color correction
  • Represent low-light features: feature representation, optical flow, and motion estimation under low light
  • Serve downstream tasks: enhancement and feature computation methods for autofocusing, matching, and reconstruction
  • Combine computational imaging: integrating light fields and other modalities with low-light scenarios
  • Customize deployable systems: tailored enhancement algorithms and system validation for practical applications

Key Challenges

  • Balance detail and noise: extreme low illumination risks over-smoothing or introducing artifacts
  • Align enhancement with tasks: objective mismatch leads to “better visuals, worse tasks”
  • Ensure evaluation generalization: complex distributions of real low-light data challenge evaluation and transfer

Technical Approach

  • Joint dual-domain modeling: strengthen contour, texture, and motion consistency across image and latent spaces
  • Apply task losses: constrain enhancement networks with focusing, optical flow, and matching objectives to achieve task-oriented enhancement
  • Incorporate multi-dimensional imaging: improve feature separability and stability under low-light conditions with light-field information

item.title: Depth Estimation
item.description:
Addressing both standard and degraded scenarios, this direction studies depth estimation methods that recover 3D structure from 2D observations, covering monocular vision, low-light conditions, and emerging sensing modalities such as event cameras, serving the front end of 3D perception, reconstruction, and decision-making.

Direction Overview

Depth estimation is the key link between 2D perception and 3D understanding. The lab focuses on depth models that remain stable under difficult conditions such as missing texture, poor illumination, and fast motion, and explores how semantic information and multimodal sensing complement geometric estimation, providing reliable 3D cues for subsequent reconstruction, navigation, and interaction.

Research Topics

  • Estimate monocular depth: monocular depth estimation with semantically guided geometric reasoning
  • Handle degraded scenarios: robust depth estimation under low light and low texture
  • Fuse event cameras: event-camera depth estimation and multimodal fusion with conventional cameras
  • Constrain depth consistency: scale recovery and uncertainty modeling for depth results
  • Validate downstream tasks: application validation for reconstruction, focusing, and scene understanding

Key Challenges

  • Scale ambiguity: geometric ambiguity in monocular settings
  • Boundary degradation: detail loss caused by low light and motion blur
  • Heterogeneous alignment: spatio-temporal alignment and fusion strategies across RGB / event sensors
  • Error propagation: propagation and controllability of depth errors in downstream tasks

Technical Approach

  • Introduce semantic priors: improve estimation quality at structural boundaries and in planar regions
  • Design robust features: build feature representations and training strategies for low-light and event data
  • Joint multi-task learning: enhance stability and transferability of depth estimation through consistency losses

item.title: Human Action Recognition
item.description:
Focusing on human behavior understanding, this direction studies methods for recognizing and analyzing actions from videos and skeleton sequences, emphasizing spatio-temporal modeling and robustness in real-world scenarios, serving applications such as human-computer interaction, intelligent surveillance, and behavior analysis.

Direction Overview

Human action recognition requires jointly characterizing appearance, posture, and temporal dynamics. The lab works along two paths: skeleton-based representation and visual features. Skeleton sequences are computationally efficient and relatively robust to appearance changes, while visual features retain richer scene and interaction information. The two can be modeled independently or fused complementarily to improve recognition under complex actions and occlusion.

Research Topics

  • Model skeleton sequences: skeleton-based action recognition with graph convolution / temporal modeling
  • Learn spatio-temporal features: spatio-temporal feature learning and long-term dependency modeling for action sequences
  • Fuse dual-path features: complementary recognition frameworks combining visual and skeleton features
  • Strengthen robust representation: behavior understanding under occlusion, viewpoint changes, and noise
  • Validate real-world scenarios: data collection, evaluation, and system demonstrations for deployment

Key Challenges

  • Fine-grained discrimination: high inter-class similarity between actions makes separation difficult
  • Representation stability: occlusion, multiple viewpoints, and background clutter cause drift
  • Long-term dependencies: wide time spans with sparse key frames
  • Distribution gap: laboratory data differs from real deployment environments

Technical Approach

  • Model graph structures: represent joint relations with skeleton graphs, capture action dynamics with temporal networks
  • Introduce attention: combine keyframe selection to improve long-sequence modeling efficiency
  • Advance multimodal fusion: enhance real-world generalization through complementary features and data augmentation
